content: 1. The activation of beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor drugs is not predictable. Co-resistance to all fluoroquinolones and often aminoglycosides is observed. 2. Intramuscular (IM) administration is possible but must be combined with a caine anesthetic due to associated pain. 3. For Moraxella catarrhalis, the preferred treatment regimen includes Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Augmentin) in various dosages: 2 tablets orally twice daily, or 500/125 mg 1 tablet orally three times daily, or 875/125 mg 1 tablet orally twice daily. Alternatively, cephalosporins such as Cefdinir (300 mg orally every 12 hours or 600 mg every 24 hours), Cefditoren pivoxil (200–400 mg orally twice daily), Cefpodoxime proxetil (200 mg orally every 12 hours), Cefprozil (500 mg orally every 12 hours), or parenteral options like Cefoxitin (1 g every 8 hours to 2 g IV/IM every 4 hours), Cefuroxime (750–1500 mg IV/IM every 8 hours), Cefotaxime (1 g every 8–12 hours to 2 g IV every 4 hours), or Ceftazidime (1–2 g IV/IM every 8–12 hours) can be used. Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (single-strength: Trimethoprim 80 mg/Sulfamethoxazole 400 mg or double-strength: Trimethoprim 160 mg/Sulfamethoxazole 800 mg) is another option. 4. Alternative regimens for Moraxella catarrhalis include Azithromycin (500 mg IV every 24 hours), Clarithromycin (500 mg orally every 12 hours), or Telithromycin (800 mg orally every 24 hours, taken as two 400 mg tablets). 5. For Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, the preferred regimen is Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (single-strength: Trimethoprim 80 mg/Sulfamethoxazole 400 mg or double-strength: Trimethoprim 160 mg/Sulfamethoxazole 800 mg). IV treatment based on the TMP component involves 8–10 mg per kg per day divided every 6, 8, or 12 hours. 6. Alternative regimens for Stenotrophomonas maltophilia include Ticarcillin-Clavulanate (3.1 g IV every 4–6 hours, with Ticarcillin 3 g and Clavulanate 0.1 g per vial) combined with Aztreonam (1 g IV every 6 hours or 2 g IV every 8 hours). 7. Note: There is potential synergy between Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole and Ticarcillin-Clavulanate. Stenotrophomonas is a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia, particularly in patients on mechanical ventilation. 8. For Bordetella pertussis, the preferred regimen is Azithromycin 500 mg orally on day 1, followed by 250 mg every 24 hours. An alternative regimen includes Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (1–2 double-strength tablets, 800/160 mg) every 12–24 hours. 9. For anaerobes (e.g., aspiration pneumonia), the preferred regimen includes Piperacillin-Tazobactam (3.375 g IV every 6 hours for 7–10 days for gram-negative bacilli), Ticarcillin-Clavulanate (200–300 mg/kg/day IV divided every 4–6 hours, max 18 g/day), Ampicillin-Sulbactam (1500–3000 mg IV every 6 hours), Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (250–500 mg orally every 8 hours or 875 mg every 12 hours), or Clindamycin (150–450 mg orally every 6–8 hours, max 1800 mg/day). 10. Alternative regimens for anaerobes include carbapenems such as Imipenem-Cilastatin, Meropenem, or Ertapenem. 11. For Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the intensive phase involves Isoniazid (5 mg/kg/day, usual dose 300 mg/day), Rifampin (10 mg/kg/day, max 600 mg/day), Ethambutol (5–25 mg/kg/day, max 1.6 g), and Pyrazinamide (1000–2000 mg/day) daily for 2 months. 12. Alternative regimens for tuberculosis include thrice-weekly dosing of the same drugs for 2 months. 13. The continuation phase for tuberculosis involves Isoniazid (300 mg/day orally daily, 5 mg/kg/day) and Rifampin (600 mg/day orally daily, 10 mg/kg/day) for 4 months. Alternatively, these drugs can be given thrice weekly for 4 months. 14. For Yersinia pestis, the preferred regimen is Streptomycin (15 mg/kg/day, max 1 g/day) or Gentamicin (7 mg/kg/day). Alternative regimens include Doxycycline (100 mg orally/IV every 12 hours), Levofloxacin (750 mg IV every 24 hours), or Moxifloxacin (400 mg IV every 24 hours). 15. For Mycoplasma pneumoniae, the preferred regimen is Azithromycin (500 mg orally on day 1, followed by 250 mg every 24 hours) or Tetracycline (250–500 mg orally every 6 hours). Alternative regimens include Levofloxacin (750 mg IV every 24 hours) or Moxifloxacin (400 mg IV every 24 hours). 16. For Chlamydophila pneumoniae, the preferred regimen is Azithromycin (500 mg orally on day 1, followed by 250 mg every 24 hours) or Tetracycline (250–500 mg orally every 6 hours). Alternative regimens include Levofloxacin (750 mg IV every 24 hours) or Moxifloxacin (400 mg IV every 24 hours). 17. For Legionella spp., the preferred regimen is Levofloxacin (750 mg IV every 24 hours), Moxifloxacin (400 mg IV every 24 hours), or Azithromycin (500 mg orally on day 1, followed by 250 mg every 24 hours). An alternative regimen is Doxycycline (100 mg orally/IV every 12 hours). 18. For Chlamydophila psittaci, the preferred regimen is Tetracycline (250–500 mg orally every 6 hours). An alternative regimen is Azithromycin (500 mg orally on day 1, followed by 250 mg every 24 hours). 19. For Coxiella burnetii, the preferred regimen is Tetracycline (250–500 mg orally every 6 hours). An alternative regimen is Azithromycin (500 mg orally on day 1, followed by 250 mg every 24 hours). 20. For Francisella tularensis, the preferred regimen is Doxycycline (100 mg orally/IV every 12 hours). Alternative regimens include Gentamicin (7 mg/kg/day) or Streptomycin (15 mg/kg/day, max 1 g). 21. For Burkholderia pseudomallei, the preferred regimen includes carbapenems (Imipenem-Cilastatin, Meropenem, or Ertapenem) or Ceftazidime (0.5–1 g every 8 hours). Alternative regimens include Levofloxacin (750 mg IV every 24 hours), Moxifloxacin (400 mg IV every 24 hours), or Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (1–2 double-strength tablets, 800/160 mg) every 12–24 hours. 22. For Acinetobacter species, the preferred regimen includes carbapenems (Imipenem-Cilastatin, Meropenem, or Ertapenem). Alternative regimens include cephalosporin-aminoglycoside combinations, Ampicillin-Sulbactam, or Colistin (2.5–5 mg/kg/day IM/IV divided every 6–12 hours, max 5 mg/kg/day). 23. For Actinomyces spp., the preferred regimen is Penicillin V (1 g orally four times daily for 2–6 weeks). Alternative regimens include Tetracycline (500 mg orally every 6 hours) or Doxycycline (100 mg every 12 hours). Minocycline, Clindamycin, and Erythromycin have also been successful. 24. For Nocardia spp., initial intravenous therapy (induction therapy) includes Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (15 mg/kg/day IV of the trimethoprim component in 2–4 divided doses) for at least 3–6 weeks and Amikacin (7.5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours) for at least 3–6 weeks. 25. Alternative regimens for Nocardia spp. include Imipenem (500 mg IV every 6 hours) and Amikacin (7.5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours). 26. Note: If the patient is allergic to sulfonamides, desensitization should be performed when possible. If the isolate is susceptible to third-generation cephalosporins (e.g., Ceftriaxone, Cefotaxime), Imipenem can be switched to one of these agents. Selected patients who clinically improve with induction intravenous therapy and do not have CNS disease may be switched to oral monotherapy (usually after 3–6 weeks) based on susceptibility results. 27. Oral maintenance therapy for Nocardia spp. includes a sulfonamide (e.g., Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole 10 mg/kg/day of the trimethoprim component in 2–3 divided doses) and/or Minocycline (100 mg twice daily) and/or Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (875 mg twice daily).
